say.text: A man presents with a groin lump that reaches down into his scrotum.
Which hernia is most likely behind this?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Follow the sac, not the name. One sac travels inside the spermatic cord coverings; the other bulges through the back wall.
Yes. The indirect sac follows the cord down the canal, so it is the one that commonly reaches the scrotum.
Its swelling is oblique and pear-shaped, and it reduces upwards, laterally and backwards.
Tempting: the direct hernia is the one you see at the front of the groin, so the name feels like the sac that drops.
But a direct sac bulges through the back wall near the pubic tubercle and rarely reaches the scrotum.
The scrotal descent belongs to the indirect sac, which follows the cord.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recheck the link: scrotal descent goes with the indirect sac that travels in the cord.

say.text: Tempting: a femoral hernia is also a groin lump, so the name pulls the scrotal swelling towards it.
But a femoral sac sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, in the femoral canal, not in the cord.
Scrotal descent points to the indirect sac, which follows the cord.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the groin hernias by position first, then by the cord.

say.text: A 3-month-old boy has a right inguinal swelling. What is the underlying defect?

choices.label: Weak posterior wall of the canal
Transversalis fascia defect at Hesselbach's triangle

say.text: Yes. An indirect hernia in a child is congenital, arising in a patent processus vaginalis.
The process normally closes after the testis descends; when it stays open, the sac comes through the groin.
Tempting: the direct hernia comes from a weak posterior wall, so that acquired cause feels like the answer for any groin swelling.
But that acquired weakness is the direct hernia's cause. A child's indirect hernia is congenital, from a patent processus vaginalis.
A direct hernia and a child's indirect hernia do not share one cause.
If the whole process stays open down to the testis, which hernia results? And if just part of it stays open?

choices.label: Whole open: funicular; part open: complete congenital
Whole open: complete congenital; part open: funicular
Whole open: direct; part open: indirect

say.text: Yes. A whole open process reaches the testis as a complete congenital hernia; a partly open one stops above it as a funicular hernia.
Tempting: both hernias sit in the same groin, so 'whole' and 'part' get matched to the names you already know.
But 'whole' and 'part' describe the open process, not the hernia's side. A funicular hernia is the partly open one, and it stops above the testis.
A direct hernia is acquired and has no patent process at all.
After reduction, the examiner presses over the deep ring and the patient coughs.
What does an indirect hernia do?

choices.label: Reappears medial to the examiner's finger
Does not reappear while the ring is held
Bulges out lateral to the finger
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which sac comes out through the deep ring itself, the very place the finger is pressing.
Yes. The finger blocks the indirect sac's route through the deep ring, so it stays in.
Tempting: the test has a result to memorise, and it is easy to attach the 'reappears' result to the wrong sac.
But the finger blocks the indirect sac, so it does not come back. A direct sac still appears medial to the finger.
So the result to keep is 'no reappearance' for an indirect hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so picture the finger on the ring: it stops the indirect sac, not the one through the back wall.

say.text: With the deep ring occluded, a swelling bulges medial to the examiner's finger on coughing.
What type of hernia is it?
Yes. The finger blocks the indirect sac, so a swelling still bulging medial to it comes through the posterior wall.
Tempting: the finger sits on the deep ring, so the sac you link with that ring seems to be the one blocked.
But an indirect sac is the one held back by the finger. A swelling that still bulges medial to it is the direct type.
Tempting: a femoral hernia is another groin lump, so it can seem to fit a swelling near the examiner's finger.
But a femoral sac sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, not through the back wall.
A swelling still medial to the finger follows the direct pattern.
In Zieman's three-finger test, the index finger sits on the deep ring, the middle on the superficial ring and the ring finger on the saphenous opening.
An impulse felt on the middle finger suggests which hernia?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Match the finger to the ring it covers first. Then ask which sac comes out at the superficial ring rather than the deep one.
Yes. The middle finger covers the superficial ring, where a direct sac pushes out, so an impulse there suggests direct.
Tempting: the fingers are easy to recall in order, so the middle finger gets handed to the first hernia you remember.
But each finger covers a ring: index the deep ring, middle the superficial ring, ring finger the saphenous opening.
So an impulse on the middle finger is the direct hernia, and femoral belongs to the ring finger.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie each finger to its ring rather than to its place in the order.

say.text: In the invagination test, the little finger pushes the scrotal skin in, and the impulse is felt on its tip or on its pulp.
An impulse on the tip suggests which hernia?
Yes. A tip impulse suggests indirect; a pulp impulse suggests direct.
Tempting: tip and pulp sound like a matter of finger order, so the first sign you recall gets the hernia.
But the tip reads the indirect sac and the pulp reads the direct sac, so depth decides it.
Femoral is not read here; it belongs to the ring finger of Zieman's test.
Relative to the inferior epigastric vessels, which hernia enters the canal through the deep ring?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which side of the vessels the deep ring lies on, and which sac comes through the back wall instead.
Yes. The indirect sac enters through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
Tempting: 'direct' sounds like the sac that comes straight out at the front, so it gets put on the outer side of the vessels.
But a direct sac bulges through Hesselbach's triangle, the back wall, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
The deep-ring sac, lateral to the vessels, is the indirect one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the names mislead: trace each sac's route against the vessels, not its name.

say.text: Tempting: a femoral hernia is another groin lump, so it can seem to come through the same opening.
But a femoral sac sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, through the femoral canal, not the deep ring.
The deep ring belongs to the inguinal canal, where the indirect sac enters.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so place the femoral hernia below the inguinal ligament before anything else.

say.text: Laparoscopic view of an elderly man with a chronic cough. The sac comes through the back wall of the canal, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
Which hernia is this?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which wall the sac passes through, and then which side of the vessels that wall lies on.
Yes. A sac through the posterior wall, medial to the vessels, is a direct hernia.
Tempting: indirect is the name most students give first, so it becomes the default for any groin sac.
But an indirect sac enters through the deep ring, lateral to the vessels, not through the back wall.
A back-wall sac, medial to the vessels, is the direct hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the wall first: the back wall means medial to the vessels, which means direct.

say.text: Tempting: a femoral hernia is another groin lump, so a sac in the groin can seem to fit it.
But a femoral sac lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, through the femoral canal, not the back wall.
A back-wall sac, medial to the vessels, belongs to the direct hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the wall and the position before you name the hernia.

say.text: The conjoint tendon adds strength to one wall of the inguinal canal. Which pairing is correct?

choices.label: Posterior wall, reinforced laterally by internal oblique

say.text: Yes. The posterior wall is transversalis fascia, and the conjoint tendon reinforces it medially.
Tempting: the conjoint tendon sits right beside the internal oblique, so it gets filed with the anterior wall.
But the anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by the internal oblique.
The conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall, medially.
A direct sac pushes through the posterior wall of the canal. Which structure reinforces that wall medially?
Yes. The conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall medially, where a direct sac pushes through.
Tempting: the internal and external obliques are the muscles you see first in the front of the groin, so they feel like the wall's support.
But both form or reinforce the anterior wall, and the posterior wall is transversalis fascia.
The medial reinforcement of the posterior wall is the conjoint tendon.
Which description fits a direct hernia in an elderly man?

choices.label: Pear-shaped swelling that reaches the scrotum and reduces laterally
Globular swelling near the pubic tubercle, reduces straight back
Globular swelling near the pubic tubercle that regularly reaches scrotum

say.text: Tempting: a swelling in an older man's groin is easily read as the one that drops to the scrotum, so the scrotal detail pulls you across.
But a direct hernia is globular, sits near the pubic tubercle, and rarely reaches the scrotum.
The pear-shaped oblique swelling that reduces laterally and backwards is the indirect one.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the shape to the sac: globular near the tubercle is direct, pear-shaped down the cord is indirect.

say.text: Yes. A direct swelling is globular, near the pubic tubercle, and reduces straight backwards. It rarely reaches the scrotum.
A groin swelling lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Which hernia is it?

choices.label: Inguinal hernia, above and medial to the tubercle
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which canal lies below the inguinal ligament, and where the inguinal hernia's neck sits relative to the tubercle.
Yes. The femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, while the inguinal hernia lies above and medial to it.
Tempting: an inguinal hernia is the groin lump most people picture first, so the inguinal position feels like the default.
But an inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle, and the femoral hernia lies below and lateral to it.
A neck below the inguinal ligament and lateral to the tubercle points to femoral.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so place the neck against the tubercle first, then name the canal.
